Sequential network states

Volker Rudolf

2025-02-17

#Goals The goal of this analysis is to turn species phenologies into a network of community state transitions. When species co-occur, they form a community state, and each species combination is a unique state, which can occur more than once. Each state has a start and ending date, and transitions into a new state. This creates a network that we will analyze to better understand how communities change

Load packages

#Get & transform data into a transition network

get the data

We assume the data comes in the form of Dynamic Nodes from the “frog data preparation” code, i.e. each observation (row) indicates when (e.g. the day) a species appears (onset) and disappears (terminus). This can happen multiple times for a given species. So there are at least 3 columns: 1) species ID, 2) onset, 3) terminus

##organize data into community states We will create a new data frame, that includes column for each unique species combination, and additional columns that indicate when the state starts and ends. Note, in same cases this might include state without species, which we call “none” here.

##Network Structure Analysis Finally, we can look at the whole structure of the transition network. We can do this as a temporal network, or transform it into a static Markov-chain network. The second option essentially ways the transition between nodes by the frequency at which the transitions occur. Note this option looses all temporal information except for pairwise transitions.

##whole network statistics on weighted transition graphs We can now calculate a number of statistics on basic “static” weighted transition graphs, with or without weights using the basic igraph package. Statistics like betweeness(), closseness(), strength(sums up edge weights), degree(), centrality (e.g. harmonic_centrality()), etc.

###Transition-Network metrics

##Edge diversity
Transition between certain state pairs can occur more common, indicating a back and forth, while other transitions may be rare. We can think of this in term of either distributions of edges, weights, or evenness. If all transitions occur equally, then eveness of edges should be high, if some transitions are dominant and occur much more frequently, than eveness is low. So in simplest case, we can calculate this with Pielou’s eveness index.

##Burstiness We will calculate temporal distribution of events, in this case when a new state appears. This gives us a good idea of when and how changes are clumped in time or not. Values=1 indicate perfect (periodic) spacing, = 0 random, >0 clumping. Note, we need to decide if we include empty states in this calculation

##Memory Now we calculate memory, which is complementary to burstiness and examines how correlated events are. >0 indicates that short interevent follow short events, =0 means it’s random, <0 means long follow short and vice versa. Basically a 1-lag autocorrelation coefficient
